words.lemma: do-beir/do-ucci 'give', pret. pass. 3sg ('was given'); slab lemma ?tuccad
for 'on' + 3sg fem. (= fuirre 'on her'); slab lemma ?fuire

cognate: Ir. ainm ~ Gk οὔνομα/ὄνομα (*h₁nómn̥) exact; Gk θέσθαι (τίθημι) ~ Ved. dhā- (nā́ma dhā-) ~ MW dodi in 'enw a dodet arnaw' as the 'put' verb of the syntagm; the Irish slab verb is not cognate.
drift_or_renewal: Renewal of the verb in Irish: 'put' (*dʰeh₁-, lost as a free verb in Goidelic) replaced by do-beir/do-ucci 'give' (tuccad, dobert, dobreth), while the noun and the frame 'name ON the recipient' (for + suffixed pronoun) are kept. Middle Welsh keeps a 'put' verb (dodi) in the same frame ('enw a dodet arnaw'); I do not assert the disputed etymology of dodi, only its 'put/place' meaning.
shared_syntax: Name-giving syntagm: NAME (object or predicative 'as name') + verb 'put/set' (Ir. renewed 'give'), passive or with parent as subject, recipient marked as goal 'upon' the child: Ir. 'X d'ainm fuirre' (for + pron.), MW 'enw a dodet arnaw' (ar + pron.), Gk 'ἐπὶ πᾶσι τίθενται' (Od. 8.554), Gk dative 'σφι οὐνόματα θέσθαι' (Hdt.); Vedic 'nā́ma dhā-' incl. double accusative (RV 10.49.2a) and passive aorist 'nā́ma dhāyi' (RV 10.115.2a, cf. Ir. passive tuccad).
context: Both slab passages narrate the birth of children followed at once by their naming by the mother/parents: Irish (Early Modern Irish saga prose, G300013) 'doruc ingin; tuccad Sláine d'ainm fuire' (she bore a daughter; Sláine was given as name on her); Herodotus 4.10 (Scythian origin tale) the mother sets names on the sons born to her ('γενομένους τοὺς παῖδας ... οὐνόματα θέσθαι'). The retriever put these two passages in different bundles via other roots; I join them. Same scene in Od. 8.552-554 (parents put [names] on all when they give birth) and Od. 18.5 (the name his mother set); same scene with dodi in the Mabinogi (birth/baptism of Gwri, Gwern, Hyddwn, Hychdwn) and with the 'give' verb already in Old Irish Immram Maíle Dúin ('Tofuisim ... mac ... dobert ainm fair'). The congruence is not just 'a name': it is the verb class 'put/set' (where kept) and the goal 'upon' the named. This is a language-level syntagm, not a poetic formula, so prose witnesses (Herodotus, saga prose) are expected; the Irish anchor is Early Modern and the stock phrase 'dorug gein mic ⁊ tucadh X d'ainm fair' recurs in translated romances (Bevis, Octavian), but the Old Irish hits show the frame is older. Why not high: the Irish verb is renewed, so the Irish anchor carries only the noun and the frame; the identification of *h₁nómn̥ dʰeh₁- as an inherited collocation (Gk ὄνομα τίθεσθαι, Ved. nā́ma dhā-, Hitt. lāman dai-, Av. nąman- dā-) is from the literature.
phrase: *h₁nómn̥ dʰeh₁- 'put a name (on a newborn)': Ir. 'tuccad Sláine d'ainm fuire' (renewed verb) ~ Gk 'οὐνόματα θέσθαι' ~ MW 'enw a dodet arnaw' ~ Ved. 'nā́ma dhāyi'

note: Slab dominated by Early Modern Irish devotional prose (Desiderius, G208020) and Buile Suibhne/CMT with mostly unrelated Greek medical/philosophical partners. One claim (naming syntagm, medium). Considered and dropped as generic co-occurrence: BC-b6ae8 Ir. reód/sioc + sneachta ~ ON frost/sniór, OE forst/sniw, Lat. pruina/nix (Irish freely substitutes sioc; annals use the pair as weather report; OE is a Benedicite translation); BC-ef2be Ir. bleaghan na mbó ~ Gk βοῦς ἀμέλγεσθαι (only way to say 'milk cows'). Also noted but not claimable from slab partners: 'ó a bhonn go a bhathais' (BC-f7d5b, biblical a planta pedis usque ad verticem).
